Capital One.

This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump and former President Obama held dueling rallies tonight.
Trump is stumping for Republican candidates in Ohio, and Obama spoke to Democrats in Georgia.
After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which this
country is not seen in modern times, you get to say enough is enough.
We're voting for change here in Georgia.
Obama blamed congressional Republicans for not holding Trump accountable for the Iran
war, tariffs, rising prices and immigration crackdowns.
He continued to criticize Trump's focus on aesthetic changes to the White House, which
Trump defended, saying the White House is the number one symbol of our country.
Latino voters in Arizona could be key in some close congressional races.
Democrats hope frustration with the economy and immigration enforcement could help them
flip at least two seats, and Piers Ashley Lopez reports.
Latino voters helped Republicans win a slew of races in Arizona in 2024.
Jaime Malera is a Republican lobbyist in the Phoenix area, and he says many of those voters
were hoping the party would lower prices and secure the border.
But Malera says the way in which the Trump administration has carried out its policies
has since turned off a lot of those Latino voters.
I think there was a lot of agreement that there should be some strong enforcement that
takes place.
But to go in and to go into communities and just rip out individuals, I think that's
left a bad taste in a lot of Latinos' mouths.
Malera said Republicans will have to do a lot of work to win many of those voters back
before the next election cycle.
Ashley Lopez, NPR News.
A group of online activists says it has published the names, email addresses and phone numbers
of tens of thousands of Department of Homeland Security employees.
The group is calling itself Department of Peace and says it got the information through
Web Security Authentication Service, used by DHS, in a statement DHS said it was "aware
of a potential breach" and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.
Stocks gained ground today as the Federal Reserve voted to hold interest rates steady,
NPR's Scott Horsley reports investors still expect the Fed to raise rates later this year.
The Fed's rate-setting committee voted 10-2 to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged.
While prices are climbing faster than the central bank would like, most Fed policymakers
opted to wait until their next meeting in December, before weighing another rate increase.
President-Chairman Kevin Warr says the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy clip but shows
little sign of overheating.
The economy is strong.
The economy is pointing in the right direction.
Is the economy running too hot?
Is the economy running too strong?
That isn't the judgment of most of my colleagues.
The decision to hold rates steady was widely expected and Warr's comments prompted little
movement in financial markets.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
The S&P 500 and NASDAQ both rose about a quarter percent today.
This is NPR News.
During the peak of the 2025 L.A. fires, about 7 million residents were exposed to airborne
lead concentrations that exceeded 80 times the normal background level.
That's according to a study in the journal Science Advances.
Researchers found that the urban smoke had lead, arsenic and other toxic metals linked
to burning vehicles, building materials and electronics.
An award-winning Egyptian journalist has been freed from detention after paying a fine for
running an unlicensed website, but NPR's Ayaba Trial reports the journalist now faces another
trial with a penalty of imprisonment.
Lina Atala's trial lasted just a few hours, and her defense team was thrown out of the
courtroom by a judge who fined her the maximum penalty of 3 million Egyptian pounds, roughly
$54,000, for operating a website without a license.
The independent English and Arabic news platform she manages, called Medamasser, says its request
for a license has been pending for the past three years.
Still, it says the judge also ordered the website closed.
Medamasser reports Atala was released following several hours of detention after paying the
fine, only to find out that she'd been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison on
charges of publishing false news.
A retrial is slated for November.
The Committee to Protect Journalists says it's all part of an escalating assault on independent
media in Egypt.
Ayaba Thrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
South Africa says it has sent the world's longest freight train on a test run.
It's 4.7 miles long with 696 wagons, which were empty for the two-day journey from a
port to an iron ore mine in the interior of the country.
I'm Rylan Barton.
This is NPR News from Washington.
